newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia to beef up security ahead of elections.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia to beef up security ahead of elections.

text.p: Indonesian authorities said they will tighten pre-election security in the capital, one day after supporters of an ousted minority party leader marched in Jakarta in defiance of official warnings against demonstrations.
Jakarta police said on Friday they have declared war on crime and would take stern action against anyone violating the law in the run-up to the May 29 general elections.
"Police will take action against any effort to disrupt the election...regardless of (political) affiliation," Jakarta police spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Edi Aritonang told Reuters.
"It's all right if demonstrations aim to convey the people's aspirations, but of course we will take action if they lead to destruction and disruption of public order," he added.
The military has recently reiterated past warnings it would not tolerate any attempts to disrupt the poll process.
Armed troops have participated in a series of exercises in the city over the past week, dropping from helicopters to scenes of simulated rioting.

On Thursday, the official Antara news agency quoted armed forces spokesman Brigadier-General Slamet Supriadi as saying authorities "would not hesitate to take stern action" to prevent politically-motivated protests from getting out of hand.
Slamet's warning singled out supporters of ousted minority party leader Megawati Sukarnoputri.
"ABRI (the armed forces) will not hesitate to deal with groups which intend to foil the elections because the armed forces have pledged to secure the elections," he said.
Hundreds of Megawati supporters held a six-hour protest in front of parliament house on Tuesday, causing traffic jams in downtown areas.
Slamet was quoted as saying the military would not tolerate any more such demonstrations in the capital.

But on Thursday about 100 Megawati supporters ignored the warning and marched on Jakarta streets to a courthouse to present a lawsuit against Megawati rival Surjadi. However, police did not attempt to stop them.
Surjadi heads the government-backed faction of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) that ousted Megawati as party leader during a party congress last June.

Megawati supporters later protested her dismissal by occupying PDI headquarters. Surjadi supporters attacked the office on July 27, prompting a police raid on the building, in which those inside were arrested.
The suit against Surjadi asked for damages for those arrested.
Police spokesman Aritonang said an extra 4,000 policemen would be brought in to strengthen the capital's 15,000-strong police force before and during the elections.
Other officials said some 10,000 soldiers will be on duty in Jakarta until after the elections, up from the usual 4,000.
Tension has grown since the beginning of April in Central Java province after clashes between supporters of the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the ruling Golkar party.
Last year, the worst riots in the city in more than two decades erupted after the police raid on the PDI headquarters.
